episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for the week ending Friday, June twelfth, twenty twenty-six. And here's who is innovating in higher education this week.

Leading off this week's Innovation Pulse, Ohio State University hired one hundred faculty members with A.I. expertise, established six university-wide learning outcomes, and pledged to make every student A.I. fluent before graduation. But when departments were asked what that fluency should look like, The Chronicle of Higher Education reports, the number one response was that people didn't know.

The disconnect is not unique to Ohio State. Purdue University announced a mandatory A.I. working competency requirement in January. The University of Virginia took a different approach, opening an A.I. Literacy and Action Lab in its library where students and faculty bring real-world problems to solve with A.I. Leo Lo, the dean of libraries at Virginia, said there is no playbook out there, and nobody has figured it out yet.

Faculty responses range from enthusiasm to deep skepticism. Nick Kawa, an Ohio State anthropology professor, questions prioritizing what he calls shiny objects over pressing global problems like sanitation access for three point six billion people. Tina Tallon, who teaches A.I. and music composition at Ohio State, provides students with non-A.I. assignment options and hopes to take students on field trips to data centers so they can physically experience the infrastructure behind the technology.

At Virginia, students in English professor Piers Gelly's class came up with the idea to test an A.I. lesson plan using a passage from King Lear. Students working without A.I. spent the entire class deeply engaged in conversation. The group with full A.I. access was not talking at all. They thought they already had the answer.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Incoming college students are already using A.I. tools, but their understanding of how those tools work remains limited, according to new research from Auburn University. Three researchers in Auburn's Office of the Provost, working in collaboration with James Madison University, published their findings in the journal Research and Practice in Assessment. The study used the Generative A.I. Literacy Assessment Test, or GLAT, to measure incoming students' A.I. literacy levels. Stuart Miller, assistant director of Academic Data Acquisitions and Reporting at Auburn, said the study gives institutions a much-needed baseline, adding that the real work is designing curriculum and experiences that actually move those numbers. The authors call for institution-wide early A.I. literacy education that emphasizes ethical reasoning and metacognitive awareness, noting that higher education institutions cannot assume incoming students are A.I.-literate. The research team recently presented its findings at the twenty twenty-six Association for Psychological Science Annual Convention.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Community colleges play a crucial role in workforce development, but many students struggle to complete valuable credentials. A new report from Brookings examines how to improve workforce outcomes for community college students. The research shows that most community college students never complete any credential at all, and many of the credentials they do obtain lack labor market value. With the recent enactment of Workforce Pell, which expands grant eligibility to students obtaining short-term certificates with demonstrable labor market value, understanding which credentials have value matters more than ever. The report recommends that colleges better align program offerings with job availability and quality, engage more deeply with employers, offer varied work-based learning experiences, and provide robust student supports including academic advising and wraparound services. The authors also call for policy changes including outcomes-based funding and increased federal assistance for workforce development programs.

<break time="1.0s"/>

The University of Rochester's Warner School faculty are sharing practical strategies for integrating A.I. into K through twelve education. Sixty-one percent of teachers now use A.I. tools in their classrooms, nearly double the thirty-four percent in twenty twenty-three. Warner School experts emphasize that the most effective uses of A.I. support rather than replace high-quality instruction. Recommended applications include making learning more accessible through tools like Diffit, which can adjust reading levels and translate materials while keeping students focused on the same learning goals. Faculty also suggest using A.I. to create more engaging and personalized learning experiences, design creative assessment alternatives, and strengthen family communication through automated translation and simplified messaging. The school offers an Advanced Certificate in Artificial Intelligence for Educators to help teachers build practical skills for responsible A.I. use in classrooms.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Washington University researchers have developed a framework to make clinical A.I. more honest about its limitations. Graduate student Sizhe Wang, working in Professor Chenyang Lu's lab at the McKelvey School of Engineering, created a model called Clinical Uncertainty Risk Alignment, or CURA. The framework teaches clinical A.I. systems when to be confident and when to be cautious by providing more trustworthy estimates of certainty and uncertainty in predictions. Today's A.I. systems have inherent risks of error or overconfidence, which can be dangerous in healthcare settings. The CURA model addresses A.I.-human collaboration, which researchers describe as a key challenge in A.I. for healthcare today. Wang will present the findings at the Association for Computational Linguistics annual meeting in July. The research aims to improve patient safety by ensuring clinical A.I. provides more reliable uncertainty estimates when supporting medical diagnoses and treatment decisions.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Faculty and trainees at the University of Miami Miller School of Medicine have completed a one hundred-day Agentic A.I. Challenge that moved beyond chatbots into practical healthcare automation. The initiative, organized in collaboration with a major technology partner, produced working A.I. agents for clinical and administrative workflows in pathology and other medical specialties. One agent automates billing code matching, reducing a twenty-minute daily task to seconds. Another translates complex pathology reports into patient-friendly explanations at a sixth-grade reading level. A third monitors blood product expiration to reduce waste of lifesaving resources. Yanyun Wu, vice chair of innovation for the department, said the goal was to take the mystery out of the technology and allow people to safely automate repetitive, time-consuming tasks.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Medical education leaders from Mount Sinai, Stanford, and the University of Washington shared their approaches to A.I. integration at a Yale School of Medicine panel. Mount Sinai established an A.I. committee that Paul Lawrence called critical in coordinating A.I. pursuits across education, research, and clinical settings. Stanford built an A.I.-powered virtual patient platform for its medical curriculum, while the University of Washington expanded an A.I. tutoring tool across all six of its teaching sites. Panelists flagged expensive A.I. pricing models as a potential driver of technological divides between institutions. Teggin Summers from Stanford noted opportunities for cross-institutional collaboration to avoid recreating the wheel, while acknowledging a pervasive urgency to catch up with rapidly evolving A.I. technology.

<break time="1.0s"/>

The A.I. job boom is creating opportunities, but not for newcomers. New research from the A.I.-Driven Enterprise Institute finds that seventy-one percent of A.I.-related job postings by S and P five hundred companies are for senior-level positions. The study examined more than one hundred sixty-one thousand job postings on LinkedIn and found that just thirteen percent of A.I.-related openings are for junior positions. This pattern reflects companies' desire for experienced talent to navigate the fast-moving A.I. landscape, but it raises concerns about developing the next generation of A.I. professionals. The findings align with broader struggles facing younger workers, as the unemployment rate for recent college graduates stands at five point six percent, well above the overall rate of four point two percent. A Stanford University study found that employment for younger workers has been stagnant since late twenty twenty-two, with young workers in A.I.-exposed occupations suffering a six percent decline in employment between late twenty twenty-two and September twenty twenty-five.

That's this week's Innovation Pulse. Full coverage and source links at innovating higher ed dot com.
